newsitem.title: USA: Social security benefits to rise 2.9 percent in '97.
newsitem.headline: Social security benefits to rise 2.9 percent in '97.

text.p: Social Security recipients will receive a 2.9 percent cost-of-living increase in their benefit payments next year, the largest increase in four years, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday.

The increase, which will be payable starting Jan. 3, 1997, will raise the average monthly benefit payment to $745 from $724, it said. It is the largest increase since a 3.0 percent bonus was given in 1993.

On average, payments to a couple, in which both receive benefits, would rise to $1,256 monthly, against $1,220 currently. The maximum benefit for a worker retiring at age 65 in January 1997 would rise to $1,326 a month.

Social Security benefits increase automatically each year based on the rise in consumer prices from the third quarter of one year to the next. Abut 44 million elderly people receive Social Security benefits.

Supplemental Security Income benefits will also increase by 2.9 percent in 1997. These benefits are paid to about 6-1/2 million poor people who are elderly or disabled. The maximum monthly benefit under this plan will rise to $484 from $470.

Also rising in 1997 is the maximum earnings level subject to the 7.65 percent social security tax rate. Starting next year, earnings above $65,400 will not be subject to the tax. The maximum this year was $62,700.

The Social Security administration said the largest rise in benefit payments since the increase became automatic in 1975 took place in 1980, when they rose 14.3 percent. The smallest took place in 1987, when the bonus was 1.3 percent.
